sentences.text: Andromeda is our nearest large neighbor. It lies 2. 5 million light-years away and is the most distant object visible to the naked eye; the light you see today set out when there were not yet any humans on Earth.
In 1923, Edwin Hubble measured a Cepheid star here and proved that Andromeda was not part of the Milky Way, but an entirely different galaxy; overnight, the universe grew millions of times larger.
It contains 1 trillion stars and is approaching us at 110 kilometers per second. In about 4. 5 billion years it will merge with the Milky Way to form a giant elliptical galaxy.
At our final stop we will see that galaxies can collide too.
The Antennae are two spiral galaxies 45 million light-years away, passing through each other.
The encounter began about 600 million years ago.
Gravity flung two long tails of stars out into space; these are the insect antennae that give them their name.
Stars do not collide with each other, the distances between them are very large; but the gas clouds collide and compress, giving birth to billions of new stars.
Within a few hundred million years the two will turn into a single elliptical galaxy.
The future of the Milky Way and Andromeda will look exactly like this too.
Our galaxies tour has come to an end.
The Large Magellanic Cloud is the Milky Way's largest satellite galaxy.
It lies 160,000 light-years away, and from the southern hemisphere it looks to the naked eye like a broken-off piece of cloud in the sky.
Its mass is about 1 percent of ours.
Inside it are the Tarantula Nebula, the largest stellar nursery in the Local Group, and R 136 a 1, one of the most massive stars known.
The supernova that exploded here in 1987 was the first supernova visible to the naked eye in 400 years.
Within a few billion years, the Milky Way will swallow it.
Now we are leaving the Local Group and going to the heart of the Virgo Cluster, 55 million light-years away.
M87 is a giant elliptical galaxy.
It has no spiral arms; it is an enormous sphere of trillions of old, yellow stars, and more than 12,000 globular star clusters orbit around it; the Milky Way has only 150.
At its center is the first black hole ever photographed, of 6. 5 billion solar masses.
The jet shooting from this black hole stretches for 5,000 light-years and has been known since 1918.
Welcome to the galaxies tour.
First, let's look at our home from the outside.
The Milky Way is a spiral galaxy 100,000 light-years across, with a bar at its center, and it contains between 200 and 400 billion stars.
The Sun lies 26,000 light-years from the center, in a small arm called the Orion Arm, and completes one orbit around the galaxy in 230 million years.
Since the dinosaurs vanished, the Sun has completed only a quarter of this orbit.
Hidden in the bright central bulge is a black hole of 4 million solar masses.
The Small Magellanic Cloud is its smaller sibling, 200,000 light-years away.
It is an irregular galaxy; the gravity of the Large Magellanic Cloud and the Milky Way probably made it into this shapeless form.
A hydrogen bridge stretching between the two is the trace of a close encounter.
In 1912, Henrietta Leavitt studied thousands of variable stars here and discovered the period-luminosity relation of Cepheid stars.
This discovery became the first cosmic ruler that lets us measure distances in the universe.
The Sombrero Galaxy deserves its name: we are looking at this galaxy, 29 million light-years away, almost exactly from its edge.
Its extraordinarily large and bright central bulge is surrounded by a sharp dust lane; just like a wide-brimmed Mexican hat.
It hosts about 2,000 globular clusters and a black hole of 1 billion solar masses at its center.
Whether it is spiral or elliptical was debated for a long time; infrared observations showed that it is a disk embedded inside an elliptical galaxy.
The Triangulum Galaxy is the third-largest member of the Local Group. It lies 2. 7 million light-years away, and with 40 billion stars it is the little sibling of Andromeda and the Milky Way.
It has no prominent central bulge or supermassive black hole; we see its arms almost from above.
Inside it lies NGC 604, a giant star-forming region 1,500 light-years across; it is 100 times larger than the Orion Nebula.
It is probably a satellite of Andromeda and will one day join it.
